Listen to this article Share Former Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang has said he would be willing to return to lead the chipmaker if its board of directors considers his reinstatement to be in the company’s best interest. Advertisement Advertisement In his first public statement since stepping down, Huang acknowledged making serious mistakes in his personal life, apologised for the problems created for the company’s board and pledged to cooperate with its independent investigation. “I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret,” he said in a statement published on Tuesday. Huang added that he took full responsibility for his actions and was committed to cooperating with the investigation. The former chief executive also addressed the growing support for his return, saying he had received calls from Nvidia employees, investors, business partners and customers urging him to resume leadership of the company. He said many continued to reach out as Nvidia navigates technological, competitive, market and geopolitical challenges. Advertisement “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honoured to answer these calls and return as CEO,” Huang said. Read also: Naira pressure mounts as FX inflows slump, reserves fall Advertisement His statement comes less than a week after his departure following revelations about extramarital relationships, including an alleged relationship with a woman suspected by US authorities of having links to Chinese intelligence. However, a return is far from certain. Nvidia’s board has indicated that it is not currently considering reinstating Huang, despite growing calls from some employees and industry figures. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress is serving as interim chief executive while the company considers its succession options. Advertisement Advertisement The controversy has also coincided with a significant decline in Nvidia’s market value. Its shares have fallen from $214 on October 29, when the allegations first became public, to approximately $154, representing a 28.04 percent decline. That translates to a $60 loss in value for every share held at the October 29 price. While the controversy has added uncertainty around the company’s leadership, broader technology-sector weakness and market conditions may also have contributed to the decline. Huang, who co-founded Nvidia and led the company for 33 years, described it as his life’s work and said building it alongside his colleagues had been a privilege. He also expressed gratitude to those who had supported him and his family, adding that he remained committed to earning back their trust. The board’s decision will now determine whether the man who built Nvidia into one of the world’s most valuable technology companies gets another opportunity to lead it.
